audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Media and Culture bachelor studies film, television, digital media, theater and dance in their historical and social contexts.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This 2026–2027 example follows the Dutch track and illustrates the English-taught Performing Arts and Creative Technologies package. The UCR plans emphasize film and culture, participatory media and sustainability, or AI and digital society.

curriculum.routeLabel: Dutch-language track — Performing Arts and Creative Technologies

cellNotes.text: Both introduce film form, history and analysis.
Both examine how media forms and technologies change over time.
Utrecht offers a dedicated new media introduction. UCR examines related topics across media and data courses.
Both analyze television and its cultural role. UCR also studies storytelling and representation on social platforms.
Both study storytelling across cultures and periods. UCR emphasizes myth and literature.
Both examine how art makes meaning. UCR focuses on the history of art interpretation.
Both compare media forms. UCR focuses on adaptation between film and text.
Both consider how exhibitions shape meaning for audiences. UCR emphasizes museum interpretation and curatorial practice.
Utrecht introduces theater and dance as fields of study. UCR includes some performance through creative communication and art.
Both explore creative practice as communication. UCR emphasizes poetic, sonic and performance experiments.
Both study how cultural work engages public issues. UCR focuses on persuasive framing and sustainability communication.
Both develop qualitative research methods. UCR includes interviews, visual methods and thematic analysis.
Utrecht studies the philosophy of science. UCR ethics addresses related questions of responsibility.
Both examine culture in society. UCR takes a broader social-theory approach.
Both develop independent research and critical source use. Utrecht prepares a media and culture thesis. UCR applies these methods to historical inquiry.
Utrecht requires a 7.5 EC thesis. UCR independent research is optional and outside the scheduled degree.
Utrecht includes 60 EC of profiling, with at least 30 EC in a coherent package.

notes.text: Utrecht offers dedicated introductions to television, theater and dance and a four-course depth package. UCR offers related audiovisual analysis, museum studies and creative practice. Utrecht also requires a research seminar and a thesis. UCR offers optional independent research alongside its course-based plans.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

ENSSUST113.text: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

GOSPHIL212.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
